Although the full text/abstract were not available here, the paper's title clearly identifies it as the source of pipeline-parallel training techniques; GPipe is widely known to implement pipeline parallelism via splitting mini-batches into micro-batches (i.e., along the batch dimension) to keep pipeline stages utilized. Thus citing GPipe to support the claim that prior work splits along the batch dimension and relies on concurrency is appropriate.

cited_title: TeraPipe: Token-Level Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large-Scale Language Models
explanation: TeraPipe is indeed a prior pipeline-parallel method introducing token-level (sequence-dimension) pipeline parallelism within a single training sequence. Thus citing TeraPipe as an example of prior pipeline parallelization work is appropriate. (Note: because TeraPipe also exploits the sequence/token dimension, the authors should be careful if they intend to claim that PipeFusion's sequence-partitioning is wholly novel compared to TeraPipe.)

cited_title: One-Step Diffusion with Distribution Matching Distillation
explanation: The cited paper (One-Step Diffusion with Distribution Matching Distillation) presents a distillation pipeline that reduces the multi-step generative process to a single forward pass (i.e., one-step diffusion), not a 4-step distilled variant. Thus it does not support the specific claim that it is an example of a "4-step Flux.1-schnell" model; the citation is misattributed. While the paper is relevant as an example of small-step/one-step distilled models (which is topically related), it contradicts the specific labeling as a 4-step variant.
evidence_quote: Our work builds upon leading diffusion models [31,63] and introduces a simple distillation pipeline that reduces the multi-step generative process to a single forward pass. Our method is universally applicable to any diffusion model with deterministic sampling [31,72,74].
top_passage_text: Diffusion Acceleration Accelerating the inference process of diffusion models has been a key focus in the field, leading to the development of two types of approaches. The first type advances fast diffusion samplers [31,41,45,46,91], which can dramatically reduce the number of sampling steps required by pre-trained diffusion models-from a thousand down to merely 20-50. However, a further reduction in steps often results in a catastrophic decrease in performance.
